simulation_guide: Predict the activation from the token's position in the sentence: if the token is a sentence/clause-final punctuation mark (period, comma closing a clause, closing quote) or a word at a clause end, expect strong negative activation (down to -10). label: Concessive 'but/though' pivot: positive = counterargument clause, negative = its subject/contrast marker
positive_pole: The token immediately after a concessive pivot ('but', 'though', 'yet', 'however', 'despite') — i.e., the start of the counterargument/qualification clause, especially function words like 'also', 'has', 'was', 'a', 'and', 'will', 'it's', 'in', 'into', 'open', 'great', 'ways', 'inevitably', 'Irene' that open the contrasting continuation.
negative_pole: The contrast-introducing subject/determiner or the pivot's own complement that names the downside ('to', 'as', 'of', 'that', 'this', 'both', 'everything', 'term', 'though', 'may', 'But', 'However') — i.e., the token that frames the negative/counter side itself, often the noun phrase head of the drawback or the pivot's object.
simulation_guide: Scan for concessive/contrast pivots ('but', 'though', 'yet', 'however', 'despite', 'although'). The token right after the pivot (start of the counter-clause) gets a strong POSITIVE activation, especially if it's a function word or generic continuation word. The token that names the downside/contrast itself — the pivot's complement or the subject of the drawback ('to the flower', 'as well as', 'of excitement', 'that revenue', 'this program', 'both potential') — gets a NEGATIVE activation. Tokens far from any contrast structure, or in plain declarative text, sit near zero (mean ~0, std 0.04). The two poles are complementary: the same contrast event produces a positive on the counter-clause opener and a negative on the contrast-naming token.

label: Discourse connective 'not only...but/also' vs. 'beyond/along with/as well as' contrastives

negative_pole: Tokens in 'beyond X', 'along with X', 'as well as X', 'in addition to X' constructions — especially the noun/phrase right after the preposition (e.g., 'efficiency', 'purchases', 'memories', 'density', 'count', 'aside', 'religion', 'music', 'itself', 'has', 'is', 'the', ',') — i.e., the item being set aside/added as a secondary consideration
simulation_guide: Scan for discourse-level additive/contrastive connectives. If the current token is 'only', 'merely', 'alone', 'just' following 'not', or the first content word after such a phrase (including the head noun of the following clause), predict strong positive activation (often +6 to +10). If the token is the object of 'beyond', 'along with', 'as well as', 'in addition to', or a comma/auxiliary immediately after such a phrase, predict strong negative activation (-7 to -10). On ordinary prose without these connective frames, activation is near zero (mean ~0, std 0.04). The neuron is essentially a discourse-structure detector distinguishing 'not only X but Y' (positive) from 'beyond/along with X' (negative) framing.

label: Narrative past-tense event verbs vs. expository connectives
positive_pole: Strong positive activation on tokens in narrative/descriptive prose recounting dramatic, violent, destructive, or consequential past events — often past-tense verbs (had, threw, wiped, damaged, wrenched, broke) or punctuation/words marking clauses in such narratives (commas, periods, 'and', 'on', 'one', 'an', 'has'). The context is vivid, eventful, often historical or mythological storytelling with concrete actions and consequences.
negative_pole: Strong negative activation on tokens in expository, technical, instructional, or quiz-like text — connectives and function words ('of', 'a', 'as', 'by', 'the', 'and', 'during', 'over', 'following', 'ing') within factual, procedural, or statistical descriptions (biology, geography, dentistry, exam questions, demographics). The context is neutral, informational, and non-narrative.
simulation_guide: Read the surrounding context (roughly the preceding clause and sentence). If it narrates a concrete, dramatic, or destructive event in past tense (violence, disasters, wars, myth, historical incidents), the activation is strongly positive, especially at verbs, punctuation, and clause-connecting words. If the context is expository, technical, procedural, or quiz-like (factual descriptions, instructions, statistics, definitions), the activation is negative, especially at function words and connectives. On neutral, ordinary, or mixed text the activation is near zero (typical magnitude ~0.035), and the token identity itself matters less than the discourse style of the surrounding context.

negative_pole: Tokens that continue or close a list/collection enumeration itself (commas between list items, 'lists' as a repeated list word, 'with/like/that/where/them' as connectives inside list-like or catalog text, 'San Francisco' as a repeated location in a list) — i.e., the connective/punctuation tokens that stitch list items together
simulation_guide: The neuron fires strongly positive on the final content word of a noun phrase that names an item, heading, or UI element in a list-like or navigational web-page context (e.g., 'gallery', 'page', 'list', 'season', 'program', 'of X', 'for X'). It fires strongly negative on tokens that are connective or punctuation elements within an enumeration (commas between items, 'lists' repeated, 'with/like/that/where/them', repeated location names in a list). On ordinary prose sentences that are neither enumerations nor navigational boilerplate, activation is near zero. The effect is about the surrounding list/boilerplate structure, not the token's surface form alone.

label: Concessive/contrastive 'not just X but Y' constructions

Near zero on ordinary prose without contrastive framing, and on these markers when used in neutral, non-qualifying ways. The neuron seems to track the strength of a 'narrowing/qualifying' discourse move rather than the literal token.

label: Imperative/invitation discourse marker vs. epistemic-hedging copula
positive_pole: Tokens in imperative or invitation contexts: 'to' before verbs of suggestion/checking, 'says/explains' introducing quotes, 'contact/visit/apply' calls to action, 'sure/certainly/name' in persuasive or directive sentences — i.e., the token is part of a directive, recommendation, or attribution-of-speech act.
negative_pole: Copular 'is/are/was/were' and 'a/an' in hedged, uncertain, or disputed-claim contexts ('is a matter of debate', 'is not known', 'is hard to prove', 'is a mystery', 'is a challenge') — epistemic uncertainty and qualification.
simulation_guide: Positive: fire strongly when the marked token sits inside an imperative, invitation, or speech-attribution frame ('be sure to', 'wish to', 'click here to', 'says X', 'contact/visit/apply') — especially sentence-initial directives or quote-introducers. Negative: fire strongly on copular 'is/are/was' or indefinite article 'a/an' when the surrounding clause expresses uncertainty, dispute, or difficulty ('is a matter of debate', 'is not known', 'is hard to'). Near zero on ordinary declarative prose, neutral 'is' statements, and function words outside these frames. Essentially a directive-vs-hedged-epistemic register detector, likely driven by the token's role in the sentence's speech act.

simulation_guide: The neuron fires strongly positive on the first digit(s) of a page number in a bibliographic citation, particularly when the token begins a page range (followed by more digits and then an en-dash/hyphen and another number). label: Mid-word / intra-word boundary detector (subword continuation)
positive_pole: Strongly positive when the measured token is a mid-word fragment: a subword piece continuing a word started earlier (e.g. 'AC' in 'electrical', 'mould'+'ing', 'F'+'olly', 'Marshall', 'andy' in 'Sandy', 'let' in 'applet', 'ut' in 'Deut.', 'trace', 'Leap', 'building', 'stir', 'box', 'Java', 'male', 'of', 'so', ',', '3', '8', '-du'). Essentially: the token is not a natural word boundary — it's a continuation piece, a suffix, a hyphen/number fragment, or a token that splits a word.
negative_pole: Strongly negative when the measured token is a clean word-final or word-initial boundary: a whole word ending a lexical item ('about' in 'roundabout', 'used', 'was', 'and', 'write', 'compared', 'bird' in 'hummingbird', 'constructed', 'my' in 'Ptolemy', 'MLA', ','), or a newline/list-item boundary ('\n-'). These are tokens where the word boundary aligns cleanly with the token boundary.
simulation_guide: For each token, ask: does this token end mid-word (i.e., the next character continues the same word, or this token itself is a fragment of a larger word)? If yes, activation is strongly positive (roughly +7 to +10). If the token is a clean word boundary — a complete word, especially word-final before whitespace/punctuation, or a newline — activation is strongly negative (roughly -7 to -10). Tokens that are ordinary whole words in flowing text with clean boundaries on both sides tend toward negative; ambiguous cases (short function words, punctuation mid-sentence) fall in between. Near zero occurs for typical whole-word tokens in ordinary prose where boundaries are clean but not emphatic.

label: Function-word 'in/of' after abstract noun phrase, definitional context
positive_pole: The token 'in' or 'of' (or comma) following a noun phrase that names a property/attribute/quantity of something, in explanatory or definitional prose — e.g. 'the presence of X in Y', 'the magnitude of', 'the nature of', 'the difference between', 'the structure of'. Essentially a preposition/possessive linking an abstract attribute noun to its bearer.
negative_pole: The same function tokens ('in', 'of', 'a', 'system', 'for') but in contexts where the preceding phrase is a concrete entity, a proper noun, a medical/technical term being defined, or a possessive-of a specific object — i.e. the same surface token but without the abstract-attribute framing; also mid-word subword continuations like 'an'+'emia', 'cult'+'uring'.
simulation_guide: Score high (+5 to +10) when the measured token is a short function word ('in', 'of', ',', 'about', 'for') immediately following an abstract/attributive noun (presence, magnitude, nature, difference, structure, content, quality, absence) that is itself part of a definitional or explanatory clause. Score strongly negative (-5 to -10) when the same function token follows a concrete entity, proper name, or a technical/medical term being introduced/defined, or when the token is a subword fragment inside a word. Near zero for ordinary 'in/of' in neutral prose, for content words, and for function words not in an attributive construction. The neuron is essentially a syntactic-semantic detector for 'abstract-attribute + linking preposition' vs. its concrete/definitional counterpart.

label: Epistemic stance: hedging/interpretation verbs vs. direct assertion
positive_pole: Tokens in contexts of epistemic hedging, interpretation, or indirect understanding: 'is asking', 'thinks', 'as limiting', 'understanding', 'implies', 'clear', 'get', 'from', 'appear', 'Summarizing' — i.e., verbs/nouns marking inference, interpretation, or uncertainty about meaning.
negative_pole: Tokens in contexts of direct definition, quotation, or explicit assertion: '“”', 'is' in definitional statements, 'actually', 'prove', 'really', 'become', 'to' in direct reference — i.e., contexts where meaning is stated outright rather than inferred.
simulation_guide: Positive activation (~+5 to +10) occurs at tokens (often copulas, prepositions, or verbs like 'understand', 'imply', 'clear', 'get') when the surrounding context frames meaning as inferred, interpreted, or hedged ('I understand', 'this implies', 'as limiting'). Negative activation (~-5 to -10) occurs at tokens in contexts of direct quotation, definition, or explicit assertion ('the subject is “the cat”', 'cannot prove', 'actually'). Near zero on ordinary text where neither hedging-inference nor direct-definition framing is salient, or at tokens unrelated to epistemic stance.

label: Succession/inheritance after death vs. death itself as subject
positive_pole: The token immediately after a death mention where a successor/relative/property takes over — succession, inheritance, or continuation clauses ('was succeeded by', 'took over', 'became', 'assumed', 'brought out', 'left her collection', 'would pass to', 'be heir'). Often the token is a comma, 'to', 'by', 'who', 'the', or a successor's name — i.e., the connective/subject introducing the inheritor.
negative_pole: The death itself as the subject of the next clause — pronouns or nouns referring back to the deceased ('he', 'she', 'it', 'had been assassinated', 'deceased', 'will not', 'didn't') or the dying person continuing to act, i.e., the dead person remains the topic rather than being succeeded.
simulation_guide: Scan for a recent death/dying mention (died, death, killed, assassinated, deceased) within the last ~15 tokens. If the current token introduces a NEW agent who inherits, succeeds, or takes over (often a comma, 'to', 'by', 'who', 'the', or a name), expect strong positive activation. If the current token refers back to the deceased as the subject of the next action (pronoun like he/she/it, or negation like 'will not', 'didn't'), expect strong negative activation. On ordinary text with no death context, activation is near zero (mean ~0, std 0.044). Ambiguous or distant death mentions give weak/intermediate values.

negative_pole: The token 'in' in the fixed pragmatic/empirical contrast phrases 'in practice', 'in reality', 'in theory ... but in practice', 'in other words', 'in many cases', 'in detail', 'in the same way', 'in the case where' — i.e., 'in' introducing a concrete, real-world, or explanatory-contrast phrase, especially the recurring 'in practice'/'in reality' idiom in human-rights/legal-report text.

Strong negative when 'in' heads the pragmatic-contrast idioms 'in practice', 'in reality', 'in other words', 'in many cases', 'in detail', 'in the same way', 'in the case where', especially in human-rights/legal-report text. Neutral/weak for ordinary spatial/temporal uses of 'in' (e.g., 'in the room', 'in 1999') unless they fit the above patterns.
